set1.q: A 52-year-old man has spent 20 years cutting and polishing stone in a quarry. He now has progressive exertional dyspnea and a restrictive pattern on pulmonary function testing. How is his occupational exposure classified?
opts: Fumes and gases form the third exposure category, beside inorganic and organic dusts. Tell: cutting and polishing stone raises a dust of free crystalline silica, a silicate dust that causes pneumoconiosis, not a fume or gas.

The treatment-related group is radiation, methotrexate, amiodarone, nitrofurantoin and chemotherapeutics. Tell: his exposure came from 20 years of quarry work, not from any medical treatment, so it is occupational.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Occupational and environmental exposures are grouped as inorganic dusts, organic dusts and fumes or gases. Stone work releases free crystalline silica, and pneumoconiosis is caused by inhaled coal dust or various inorganic or silicate dusts, so his exposure is an inorganic dust.

Organic dusts are the hypersensitivity pneumonitis sources: moldy hay, bird excreta and feathers, moldy sugarcane pulp and other moldy products. Tell: crystalline silica from stone is a silicate dust, which places his exposure in the inorganic group.

set1.q: A 68-year-old former shipyard worker has mesothelioma confirmed on pleural fluid cytology. He asks what treatment can offer him. Which response is accurate?
opts: No treatment is known to prolong survival in mesothelioma, which is incurable with poor long-term survival. Tell: a promise of surgical cure runs against everything described for this pleural cancer, whose care is primarily supportive.
Removing the fibers stops the cancer

Asbestos fibers invade lung tissue and cannot be removed, which is why asbestos disease is treated supportively. Tell: mesothelioma is an established cancer that is incurable, with no treatment known to prolong survival.

Corticosteroids are used in sarcoidosis and in severe hypersensitivity pneumonitis, aimed at inflammation. Tell: mesothelioma care is primarily supportive, with no therapy known to prolong survival in this pleural cancer.
Supportive care, as it is incurable

Correct. Mesothelioma is incurable with poor long-term survival; no treatment is known to prolong survival, and care is primarily supportive. His shipyard history fits, since mesothelioma is nearly always caused by asbestos exposure, a 10% lifetime risk for asbestos workers.

set1.q: A 58-year-old man is found to have interstitial lung disease on computed tomography after months of exertional dyspnea and dry cough. No cause has been identified yet. Which step comes first in looking for a known cause?
opts: A detailed job and hobby history

Correct. Known causes come from occupational and environmental exposures, inorganic dusts, organic dusts and fumes or gases, and from treatments such as radiation, methotrexate, amiodarone and nitrofurantoin. Asbestosis, silicosis and hypersensitivity pneumonitis each start from an exposure history, so the history comes first.

Idiopathic fibrosing interstitial pneumonia may require biopsy, but idiopathic disease is diagnosed only when no associated cause is evident. Tell: an exposure revealed by the history changes the diagnosis before any tissue is taken.

Corticosteroids are used for set indications, such as sarcoidosis with hypercalcemia or severe hypersensitivity pneumonitis. Tell: treating before the cause is known skips the step that identifies an exposure to remove, the first treatment in hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

Serum antibodies to an agent give the definitive diagnosis of hypersensitivity pneumonitis once a specific exposure, such as birds, is suspected. Tell: no exposure has been identified yet; the history is what names the agent to test for.

set1.q: A 49-year-old man with acute respiratory distress syndrome after severe pancreatitis is now hemodynamically stable on the ventilator. Which fluid strategy is preferred?
opts: Inotrope-driven excessive oxygen delivery causes potential harm, so supranormal targets are avoided. Tell: the preferred hemodynamic strategy is restrictive fluids, not pushing oxygen delivery above normal with drugs.
Fluids guided by a routine artery catheter

Routine pulmonary artery catheters offer no clinical benefit in acute respiratory distress syndrome. Tell: fluids follow a conservative protocol, and cardiac function is assessed with echocardiography rather than a catheter.

Correct. A conservative fluid protocol, targeting a central venous pressure under 4 mm Hg, is preferred, and restrictive fluids significantly increase ventilator-free days and shorten intensive care stays. His hemodynamic stability allows that restrictive approach.
Liberal fluids to support oxygen delivery

Liberal fluids run against the conservative protocol that increases ventilator-free days. Tell: the preferred strategy is restrictive, with a low central venous pressure target, once the patient is hemodynamically stable like him.

set1.q: A 52-year-old man has acute bird fancier's lung from the pigeons he keeps at home, and his symptoms are settling. He asks whether he can keep the birds if he takes medicine whenever symptoms flare. Which counsel is accurate?
opts: Corticosteroids may help severe cases, but treatment starts with avoiding the agent. Tell: no medicine is described as making continued exposure safe, and continued exposure may worsen the disease toward its chronic form.
His lung damage is already permanent

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis symptoms can be reversible if caught early, and acute disease shows little change on imaging. Tell: his acute illness is settling, so his outcome still depends on removing the birds now.

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is a non-atopic, non-asthmatic inflammatory disease from inhaled organic dust. Tell: his reaction is to the bird antigen itself, so treating it as asthma leaves the exposure in place.
Continued exposure may worsen his disease

Correct. Prompt diagnosis is key so the patient can be removed from the irritating environment: symptoms can be reversible if caught early, but continued exposure may lead to a worsened disease state. Treatment starts with identifying and avoiding the agent, here his birds.

set1.q: A 58-year-old woman has 8 months of progressive exertional dyspnea and a persistent nonproductive cough, with bibasilar dry rales and small lung volumes on examination. Which combination of total lung capacity and ratio of forced expiratory volume in 1 second to forced vital capacity is expected?
opts: This is the reverse of the restrictive pattern, in which the ratio is normal or increased and total lung capacity is decreased. Tell: scarred, stiff lungs shrink, matching her small lung volumes on examination, rather than holding more air.

A low ratio does not fit the restrictive pattern, which keeps the ratio normal or increased. Tell: interstitial disease also lowers total lung capacity, so a normal capacity misses the defining change in her stiff, small lungs.

Normal values would miss the restriction that scarring produces once lung tissue stiffens. Tell: an examination can be normal early in the disease, but her small lung volumes and progressive dyspnea point to a reduced total lung capacity.
Low capacity, normal or high ratio

Correct. Interstitial lung disease stiffens the lung so it no longer expands, giving a restrictive pattern: total lung capacity and forced vital capacity fall while the ratio of forced expiratory volume in 1 second to forced vital capacity stays normal or rises. Her small lung volumes on examination fit.

set1.q: A 35-year-old man with stable sarcoidosis is planning his yearly follow-up. He will have a physical examination, pulmonary function testing, a chest film, an electrocardiogram and a chemistry panel. Which referral completes his yearly evaluation?
opts: Lung transplant may be indicated in severe coal workers' pneumoconiosis and is listed among hypersensitivity pneumonitis treatments. Tell: his disease is stable, and the yearly referral every patient with sarcoidosis needs is an eye examination.

Correct. Patients with sarcoidosis require a yearly physical examination, pulmonary function testing, chest film, electrocardiogram, chemistry panel and ophthalmologic evaluation. The eye examination identifies and manages ocular inflammation, which matters because iritis and uveitis are indications for corticosteroids.

Transbronchial lung or fine-needle node biopsy confirms sarcoidosis by showing noncaseating granulomas, a one-time diagnostic step. Tell: yearly follow-up lists an examination, function tests, a film, an electrocardiogram, chemistry and an eye evaluation, not repeat biopsy.

Bronchoalveolar lavage appears among the diagnostic studies for idiopathic interstitial pneumonia and shows milky fluid in silicosis. Tell: it is not part of yearly sarcoidosis follow-up, which instead adds an ophthalmologic evaluation for ocular inflammation.

set1.q: A 50-year-old woman with moderate acute respiratory distress syndrome from sepsis is on low tidal volume ventilation. A colleague proposes changing the ventilator strategy. Which change should be avoided?
opts: Correct. High-frequency oscillatory ventilation provides no proven benefit in acute respiratory distress syndrome and is listed among the approaches to avoid. Her moderate disease is better served by low tidal volumes, careful positive end-expiratory pressure titration and early prone positioning.

Early prone positioning decreases mortality in moderate to severe acute respiratory distress syndrome. Tell: she has moderate disease, so positioning is a step to take, not one to avoid, and it pairs with her low tidal volumes.

Positive end-expiratory pressure is titrated carefully to maintain an arterial oxygen tension above 60 mm Hg. Tell: careful titration is part of standard ventilation in this syndrome, not something to avoid.

Low tidal volume ventilation is the strategy behind the 30% baseline mortality figure for acute respiratory distress syndrome. Tell: it is the foundation of her ventilation, so continuing it is correct rather than a change to avoid.

set1.q: A 70-year-old woman with no exposures, drug history or connective tissue disease has 18 months of insidious dry cough and exertional dyspnea. She has bibasilar inspiratory crackles and clubbing, pulmonary function testing shows a restrictive pattern, and chest films over several years show progressive fibrosis. No computed tomography has been done. What is the next step?
opts: Serum antibodies to an inhaled agent

Serum antibodies to the agent definitively diagnose hypersensitivity pneumonitis, which follows organic dust exposure. Tell: she has no exposures to test for, and the step that completes her workup is computed tomography.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Past age 65 she already meets three of the four criteria: idiopathic disease with inspiratory crackles, restrictive physiology and progressive radiographic fibrosis. Diffuse, patchy fibrosis with pleural-based honeycombing on high-resolution computed tomography would complete the set, making idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis 90% certain without biopsy.

Surgical lung biopsy is not needed in a patient over 65 who meets all four criteria, and she may meet them once the scan is done. Tell: her missing criterion is a computed tomography finding, so the scan comes before any biopsy is considered.

An elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme level is seen in 40-80% of patients with sarcoidosis, whose onset is in the third and fourth decades. Tell: her age, clubbing and years of progressive fibrosis fit idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, and the remaining criterion is a scan finding.

set1.q: A 19-year-old man is resuscitated after a near-drowning. Within 24 hours he has refractory hypoxemia and new bilateral opacities on chest film with a normal heart size, and an echocardiogram shows normal cardiac function. On the ventilator his arterial oxygen pressure is 54 mm Hg on a fraction of inspired oxygen of 0.60. How is his oxygenation impairment classified?
opts: The criterion is met whenever the ratio of arterial oxygen pressure to fraction of inspired oxygen is under 300 mm Hg. Tell: 54 / 0.60 = 90, far below 300, so he clearly meets the oxygenation criterion and sits in the worst class.

Mild is a ratio of 200-300 mm Hg, the least impaired class that still meets the criterion. Tell: his ratio of 54 / 0.60 = 90 is less than half the bottom of the mild range, two classes worse than mild.
Moderate covers 100-200 mm Hg. Tell: 54 / 0.60 = 90 falls just under 100, which crosses into the severe class; rounding up toward 100 is the mistake that makes moderate look right.

Correct. Divide arterial oxygen pressure by fraction of inspired oxygen: 54 / 0.60 = 90 mm Hg. A ratio under 100 is the severe class. Near-drowning is a direct pulmonary insult, and new bilateral opacities within a day with a normal heart complete the criteria.

set1.q: A 71-year-old man has taken amiodarone for atrial fibrillation for 6 years. Over several months he has developed progressive exertional dyspnea, a dry cough and bibasilar inspiratory crackles, and pulmonary function testing shows a restrictive pattern. He has no occupational exposures. How is his interstitial lung disease classified?
opts: Correct. Amiodarone sits with radiation, methotrexate, nitrofurantoin and chemotherapeutics in the treatment-related group of interstitial lung disease of known cause. His exertional dyspnea, dry cough, crackles and restrictive pattern fit interstitial disease, and his years of amiodarone supply the cause.

Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is the diagnosis only when no associated cause is evident, even in a patient over 65 with crackles and restriction. Tell: amiodarone is an associated cause in his history, so his disease cannot be called idiopathic.

The occupational group of known cause includes asbestosis and silicosis, which need years of work exposure to asbestos fibers or silica dust. Tell: he has no occupational exposure; the known cause in his history is a medicine he takes.
ruled out by a stated finding

Granulomatous lung disease covers sarcoidosis and hypersensitivity pneumonitis, where organized granulomas form in response to inflammation. Tell: nothing in his history points to granulomas or an inhaled organic antigen; his medicine list points to a drug cause.

set1.q: A 41-year-old man with a dry cough and exertional dyspnea is being evaluated for interstitial lung disease. Which chest film finding would point toward sarcoidosis or silicosis rather than idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis?
opts: Progressive fibrosis over several areas, built up over several years, is the chest film of idiopathic fibrosing interstitial pneumonia and one of the criteria for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Tell: it supports idiopathic fibrosis rather than moving away from it.
Pleural plaques at the lung bases

Pleural plaques, with linear streaking at the bases, are the most common chest film finding in asbestosis. Tell: plaques point to asbestos exposure, while hilar and mediastinal lymph node enlargement points to sarcoidosis or silicosis.

Correct. Hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy on a chest film points to sarcoidosis or silicosis. Sarcoidosis shows symmetric bilateral hilar and right paratracheal adenopathy, and silicosis can show eggshell calcification of the periphery of the hilar lymph nodes.
Increased markings in the lower lung fields

Increased interstitial markings in the lower lung fields are the radiograph of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Tell: that finding favors the diagnosis the question asks you to move away from; lymph node enlargement points to sarcoidosis or silicosis.

set1.q: A 66-year-old man is recovering after 3 weeks in the intensive care unit for acute respiratory distress syndrome. He has muscle wasting, weakness and persistent fatigue. Which referral addresses these problems?
opts: Yearly ophthalmologic evaluation is sarcoidosis follow-up for ocular inflammation. Tell: his needs after intensive care are muscle strength and fatigue, which rehabilitation addresses, not eye monitoring.

Correct. Long-term recovery after acute respiratory distress syndrome includes treating physical sequelae: post-intensive care muscle wasting, weakness and persistent fatigue. Rehabilitation addresses them while his lung function continues to improve over 6 to 12 months.

Lung transplant is listed for severe coal workers' pneumoconiosis and hypersensitivity pneumonitis. Tell: his problems are muscle wasting and weakness after intensive care, while his lungs are still recovering on their usual timeline.

Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation is a salvage option for severe, refractory disease during the acute illness. Tell: he is in recovery, and his problems are physical sequelae of intensive care, not refractory hypoxemia.

set1.q: A 49-year-old coal miner is told he has simple coal workers' pneumoconiosis. He asks whether a medicine can cure it. Which response is accurate?
opts: Coal macules form when alveolar macrophages take up inhaled coal dust; they are dust deposits, not an infection. Tell: management of coal workers' pneumoconiosis is supportive, and no curative treatment is available by any drug.
Leaving the mine reverses the scarring

Fibrosis is permanent scar tissue that damages the alveoli, so stopping exposure does not undo it. Tell: the disease whose symptoms can reverse when caught early and the exposure removed is hypersensitivity pneumonitis, not pneumoconiosis.

Bronchodilators are supportive treatment in hypersensitivity pneumonitis and do not act on inhaled coal dust. Tell: management of coal workers' pneumoconiosis is supportive, and no effective curative treatment is available.

Correct. Coal workers' pneumoconiosis has no effective curative treatment, and care is supportive: oxygen, pneumococcal and influenza vaccinations, rehabilitation and smoking cessation, with lung transplant in severe cases. Fibrosis, once formed, is permanent scar tissue.

set1.q: A 34-year-old man has bilateral hilar adenopathy on chest film and sarcoidosis is suspected, but his clinical and radiographic findings also raise the possibility of lymphoma. What is the next step?
opts: Angiotensin-converting enzyme is elevated in only 40-80% of patients with sarcoidosis, so it can support but not settle the diagnosis. Tell: when findings suggest an alternative diagnosis such as lymphoma, biopsy is the step named as essential.
Repeat chest film in a year

Yearly chest films belong to sarcoidosis follow-up once the diagnosis is made. Tell: waiting a year leaves possible lymphoma undiagnosed; the findings that raise lymphoma make biopsy essential now rather than later.

Correct. Biopsy is essential whenever clinical and radiographic findings suggest an alternative diagnosis such as lymphoma. Transbronchial lung or fine-needle node biopsy also confirms sarcoidosis itself by showing noncaseating granulomas, so tissue settles the question either way.

Corticosteroids treat sarcoidosis once it is confirmed and an indication such as hypercalcemia or uveitis is present. Tell: with lymphoma still possible, the diagnosis is unsettled, and biopsy is essential before treatment begins.

His chest film shows new bilateral opacities not explained by effusion, atelectasis or nodules, and an echocardiogram shows normal cardiac function. His arterial oxygen pressure is 62 mm Hg on a fraction of inspired oxygen of 0.40. How is his oxygenation impairment classified?
opts: The oxygenation criterion is a ratio of arterial oxygen pressure to fraction of inspired oxygen under 300 mm Hg. Tell: 62 / 0.40 = 155, well under 300, so he meets the criterion and the question becomes which class.
Mild covers ratios of 200-300 mm Hg. Tell: his ratio, 62 / 0.40 = 155, is below 200, one class worse than mild; reading 62 against 300 without dividing by 0.40 is what makes mild look right.

Correct. Divide arterial oxygen pressure by fraction of inspired oxygen: 62 / 0.40 = 155 mm Hg. That is under the 300 threshold and falls between 100 and 200, the moderate class. Severe pancreatitis is a systemic trigger, and his new opacities and normal heart complete the criteria.

Severe is a ratio under 100 mm Hg, the class with the most impaired oxygenation. Tell: 62 / 0.40 = 155 sits above 100, so he has not reached the severe class; an arterial oxygen pressure of 62 alone is not the ratio.

set1.q: A 58-year-old stone worker with silicosis still uses cigarettes daily. He is on oxygen therapy and has had his vaccinations. Which additional measure belongs in his treatment?
opts: Correct. Treatment of silicosis is largely supportive: oxygen therapy, physiotherapy, medications and vaccinations, plus smoking cessation. With oxygen and vaccines already in place, stopping cigarettes is the measure still missing from his plan.

Bronchoalveolar lavage in silicosis is a diagnostic study that shows a thick, milky effluent with foamy macrophages. Tell: his treatment is supportive, and the piece missing from his plan is stopping cigarettes, not a procedure.

Infliximab is used for corticosteroid-intolerant or refractory sarcoidosis, with methotrexate and azathioprine. Tell: silicosis treatment is supportive, and his remaining modifiable factor is daily cigarette use, not granulomatous inflammation.

Early prone positioning decreases mortality in moderate to severe acute respiratory distress syndrome on a ventilator. Tell: he has chronic silicosis, not an acute ventilated syndrome, and his missing measure is smoking cessation.

set1.q: A 63-year-old woman has kept birds for decades. Over 2 years she has developed a persistent cough, shortness of breath and weight loss, and she now has clubbing of the fingers. Which finding places her hypersensitivity pneumonitis in the chronic form rather than the subacute form?
opts: Cough runs through all three forms, acute, subacute and chronic. Tell: it is the least specific of her findings; clubbing of the fingers marks the chronic form, which develops from multiple exposures.

Correct. Clubbing of the fingers or toes is marked only for chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis, alongside fatigue and lung fibrosis, after multiple exposures. Cough, shortness of breath and weight loss are shared by the subacute and chronic forms, so they cannot separate the two.

Anorexia or weight loss is marked for both subacute and chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis. Tell: a finding shared by both forms cannot separate them; clubbing of the fingers or toes is the chronic-only sign in her history.

Shortness of breath is present in both the subacute and the chronic form. Tell: the signs that belong to the chronic form alone are clubbing, fatigue and lung fibrosis, and clubbing is the one she has.

set1.q: A 57-year-old stone worker has had silicosis for 8 years. He asks which complication his lung disease puts him at increased risk of. Which is it?
opts: Correct. Silicosis carries an increased risk of tuberculosis, together with progressive massive fibrosis and scleroderma. That is why patients with silicosis should have a tuberculosis skin test and a current chest film, and why the risk deserves mention at follow-up.

Mesothelioma, a primarily pleural cancer, is nearly always caused by asbestos exposure, with a 10% lifetime risk in asbestos workers. Tell: his dust is silica from stone work, whose listed complications are tuberculosis, massive fibrosis and scleroderma.

Hypercalcemia occurs in about 5% of patients with sarcoidosis and is an indication for corticosteroids there. Tell: silica dust causes silicosis, not sarcoidosis, and silicosis complications are tuberculosis, progressive massive fibrosis and scleroderma.

Goodpasture syndrome is glomerulonephritis with diffuse pulmonary hemorrhage in young adults, identified by basement membrane antibodies. Tell: it is not a silica complication; silicosis raises the risk of tuberculosis.

opts: Correct. His age, hemoptysis, hemorrhage and kidney findings fit that pairing.

A high antinuclear antibody points to collagen vascular diseases such as lupus and rheumatoid arthritis. Tell: lung hemorrhage with glomerulonephritis in a young adult is the Goodpasture pattern, identified by basement membrane antibodies instead.

A positive cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody points to granulomatosis with polyangiitis, a granulomatous vasculitis. Tell: the pairing of glomerulonephritis and diffuse pulmonary hemorrhage in a young adult is described for Goodpasture syndrome.

opts: Nontender lymphadenopathy is a sarcoidosis symptom and does not appear on the corticosteroid indication list. Tell: of her four findings, the facial skin sores are the one that meets a listed indication, as a cutaneous lesion other than erythema nodosum.

Correct. Cutaneous lesions other than erythema nodosum are an indication for oral corticosteroids, and lupus pernio, the painful skin sores on her face, is such a lesion. Erythema nodosum is the one skin finding the indication list leaves out by name.

Erythema nodosum is a sarcoidosis skin finding, but the indication reads cutaneous lesions other than erythema nodosum. Tell: her rash on the lower legs is excluded by name, while her facial skin sores are not, so the sores carry the indication.

Parotid gland enlargement is an examination finding of sarcoidosis, but it is not among the listed corticosteroid indications. Tell: the indications include hypercalcemia, eye, heart and nervous system involvement, progressive lung lesions and skin lesions other than erythema nodosum.

Her calcium is normal, and she has no eye, heart or nervous system involvement. She asks for oral corticosteroids to treat the rash. Which response is accurate?
opts: Her rash is not a steroid indication

Correct. The skin indication for oral corticosteroids is cutaneous lesions other than erythema nodosum, so erythema nodosum itself does not qualify. She has none of the other indications, such as hypercalcemia, iritis, uveitis, cardiac or nervous system involvement or progressive pulmonary lesions.
Any sarcoid skin rash needs steroids

The skin indication excludes erythema nodosum by name: it reads cutaneous lesions other than erythema nodosum. Tell: lupus pernio on the face would qualify, but her rash on the lower legs does not, and she has no other indication.
Steroids wait until other drugs fail

The order runs the other way: corticosteroids come first, and methotrexate, azathioprine or infliximab are used for patients intolerant of corticosteroids or refractory to them. Tell: steroids are held for a listed indication, not held back for drug failure.
Stage I disease needs steroids early

Stage I, bilateral hilar adenopathy alone, carries the best prognosis, and the lung indication for corticosteroids is progressive pulmonary lesions. Tell: her stage I film shows no parenchymal disease at all, let alone progression.

opts: Asbestos disease does not usually surface within a year; the course runs 10-20 years, with care sought at about 15. Tell: illness within hours of each exposure fits hypersensitivity pneumonitis from organic dust, not asbestos.

Five years is well short of the usual course: patients usually seek medical attention about 15 years after asbestos exposure. Tell: the timeline to remember is 10-20 years, centered on 15, so 5 years is too early.

Correct. Asbestosis develops over 10-20 years, and patients usually seek medical attention about 15 years after exposure. That long delay is why an exposure history matters in an older patient with dyspnea, and why a young worker's risk starts with exposure he has now.

Forty years overshoots the usual interval of about 15 years from asbestos exposure to seeking care. Tell: asbestosis is described as a 10-20 year process, not one that waits a working lifetime to appear.

opts: Sedatives, analgesics and antipyretics reduce oxygen demand in acute respiratory distress syndrome and are used appropriately. Tell: they are part of care, while the routine catheter is what offers no clinical benefit.

Correct. Routine pulmonary artery catheters offer no clinical benefit in acute respiratory distress syndrome and are avoided. Cardiac function is assessed by echocardiography to exclude hydrostatic cardiogenic edema, and he has already had one showing normal function.

A conservative fluid protocol, targeting a central venous pressure under 4 mm Hg, increases ventilator-free days. Tell: restrictive fluids are recommended in this syndrome, not avoided, and his stability allows them.
Transfusing at a hemoglobin of 7 g/dL is the recommended threshold, because higher hemoglobin targets do not improve outcomes. Tell: this threshold is part of care, not a practice to avoid.

set1.q: A 76-year-old man has had interstitial lung disease for 9 years, and his dyspnea now occurs at rest. An echocardiogram shows right heart failure. What does the right heart failure indicate about his lung disease?
opts: Cardiogenic pulmonary edema displays cardiomegaly, vascular engorgement and batwing perihilar opacities, a hydrostatic problem of the heart rather than scarred lung. Tell: his right heart failure follows 9 years of lung disease, the pattern of advanced interstitial disease.
It has entered an acute phase

An acute presentation develops over days to weeks, while most interstitial lung diseases present chronically over months to years. Tell: a 9-year course ending in right heart failure is chronic, advanced disease, not a new acute phase.
It is at an advanced stage

Correct. Right heart failure appears with advanced interstitial lung disease, and dyspnea that has spread from exertion to rest also marks progression. Early in the disease the examination may be normal, so these findings place him late in a long, chronic course.
It is at an early stage

Early disease may show a normal examination and exertional symptoms only. Tell: dyspnea at rest and right heart failure are features of progression and advanced disease, the opposite end of his 9-year course from the early stage.

opts: Correct. Management of coal workers' pneumoconiosis is supportive, with oxygen, vaccinations, rehabilitation and smoking cessation, and in severe cases lung transplant may be indicated. He has severe disease that is worsening despite every supportive measure on the list.

No effective curative treatment is available, and the listed management is supportive care with lung transplant for severe cases. Tell: removing the dust is not among the options described; replacing the lung is the step named for severe disease.

Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation is a salvage option reserved for severe, refractory acute respiratory distress syndrome. Tell: his disease is chronic dust-related fibrosis, for which the severe-case option is lung transplant, not acute salvage support.

Yearly ophthalmologic evaluation is part of sarcoidosis follow-up, to find and manage ocular inflammation. Tell: coal workers' pneumoconiosis has no eye monitoring step, and his severe, worsening lung disease points to transplant evaluation.

She now has progressive exertional dyspnea, a dry cough, bibasilar inspiratory crackles and a restrictive pattern on pulmonary function testing. She asks whether her arthritis medicine could be involved. Which response is accurate?
opts: Methotrexate, a common treatment for rheumatoid arthritis and lupus, is in the treatment-related group of interstitial lung disease causes. Tell: her years of methotrexate are a recognized cause of exactly this disease, so the medicine cannot be dismissed.
No, drug injury needs cancer chemotherapy

The drug causes reach beyond chemotherapy: the treatment-related group includes methotrexate, amiodarone and nitrofurantoin as well as chemotherapeutics. Tell: methotrexate is named in that group in its own right, whatever disease it is given for.
Yes, methotrexate deposits dust in the lungs

Dust deposition in the alveoli is how silica and coal cause pneumoconiosis, through macrophage invasion and fibrosis. Tell: methotrexate is a drug cause in the treatment-related group, not an inhaled dust, so the mechanism offered is wrong.
Yes, methotrexate can cause this disease

Correct. Methotrexate is used for many autoimmune diseases, including lupus and rheumatoid arthritis, and it has also been implicated as a cause of interstitial lung disease. Rheumatoid arthritis is itself a connective tissue cause, so her disease and her treatment both belong in the differential.

set1.q: A 54-year-old man with newly diagnosed interstitial lung disease asks how the inflammation in his lungs turns into scar tissue. Which sequence is accurate?
opts: This runs the chain backward: collagen is the end product that forms the scar, not the starting event. Tell: the sequence begins with inflammatory cells gathering in the alveolar walls, which is alveolitis, and ends with collagen laid down as fibrosis.

Fibroblasts do not start the process; they are produced in response to alveolitis. Tell: inflammatory cells in the alveolar walls create the alveolitis first, the fibroblasts follow, and their collagen comes last as permanent scar.

Collagen is made by the fibroblasts, so it cannot appear before them. Tell: alveolitis leads to fibroblast production, and those fibroblasts then produce the collagen that causes fibrosis, the stiff scar that impairs gas exchange.

Correct. Macrophages, lymphocytes, monocytes and neutrophils accumulate in the alveolar walls, producing alveolitis. Alveolitis leads to fibroblast production, and the collagen the fibroblasts produce causes the fibrosis: permanent scar tissue that stiffens the lung and impairs gas exchange.

opts: A surgical lung biopsy is a diagnostic test, and patients over 65 who meet the four criteria do not need one. Tell: biopsy defines the disease rather than removing it, and fibrosis is permanent scar tissue spread across the lungs.

Correct. Management of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is controversial: nothing has been shown to improve survival or quality of life compared with no treatment. Accurate diagnosis helps identify patients who may benefit from available therapies, and her smoking cessation remains critical to prolonging life.

Fibrosis is permanent scar tissue, and corticosteroids are reserved for a few rare idiopathic pneumonia subtypes. Tell: in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis nothing, steroids included, has improved survival compared with no treatment.

Methotrexate is used for corticosteroid-intolerant sarcoidosis and is itself implicated as a cause of interstitial lung disease. Tell: in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis nothing has improved survival compared with no treatment, and this drug can injure the lung itself.

He has clubbing, bibasilar inspiratory crackles, tachypnea and reduced chest expansion. Computed tomography shows diffuse, patchy fibrosis with pleural-based honeycombing. He has no occupational exposures, medicines or connective tissue disease. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Sarcoidosis brings noncaseating granulomas, bilateral hilar adenopathy and onset in the third and fourth decades. Tell: a 69-year-old smoker with pleural-based honeycombing and no adenopathy described fits idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis follows inhaled organic dust, such as moldy hay or bird excreta, with malaise, chills and fever hours after exposure. Tell: he has no exposure, and his disease came on insidiously over 18 months.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Insidious dry cough, exertional dyspnea, fatigue, clubbing, bibasilar inspiratory crackles, tachypnea and reduced chest expansion are the picture of idiopathic fibrosing interstitial pneumonia, and pleural-based honeycombing with no associated cause is idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Most patients have a smoking history.

Asbestosis follows years of asbestos exposure in insulation, demolition, shipyard or construction work, with pleural plaques as its most common film finding. Tell: he has no occupational exposure, so there is no asbestos source.

opts: Serum antibodies to an inhaled agent

Serum antibodies to the agent definitively diagnose hypersensitivity pneumonitis, which follows organic dust. Tell: demolition work is an asbestos exposure, and laboratory studies are not helpful in asbestosis; imaging is.

Correct. Asbestosis imaging is often normal, especially early, so a normal chest film does not exclude it, and laboratory studies are not helpful. Computed tomography is the preferred imaging for asbestosis, showing pleural plaques, alveolitis or fibrosis, and honeycombing in advanced disease.
Repeat chest film in a year

The chest film is often normal early in asbestosis, so repeating it a year later only delays the answer. Tell: computed tomography is the preferred imaging and can show plaques, alveolitis or fibrosis now, while his symptoms are active.

Bronchoalveolar lavage returning thick, milky fluid with foamy macrophages is a silicosis finding. Tell: for suspected asbestosis after demolition work, the preferred next study is computed tomography, not lavage.

opts: Stage I is bilateral hilar adenopathy alone, the stage with the best prognosis. Tell: honeycombing and hilar retraction are signs of fibrosis, which stage I lacks entirely, so his film is far beyond stage I.
Stage II is hilar adenopathy with parenchymal involvement. Tell: his hila are retracted by scarring rather than enlarged, and honeycombing marks advanced fibrosis, not the infiltrates of stage II.

Stage III is parenchymal involvement alone, seen as diffuse reticular infiltrates. Tell: honeycombing, hilar retraction and bullae go beyond infiltrates to advanced fibrosis, the defining feature of stage IV.

Correct. Stage IV is advanced fibrosis with evidence of honeycombing, hilar retraction, bullae, cysts and emphysema, which his film shows. About 20% of patients with lung involvement experience irreversible lung impairment from progressive fibrosis, bronchiectasis and cavitation.

opts: Yes, by acting as an inhaled dust

Inhaled inorganic dusts, organic dusts and fumes make up the occupational and environmental group, as in silicosis or farmer's lung. Tell: radiation belongs to the treatment-related group, not to the inhaled exposures, so the mechanism offered is wrong.
Yes, radiation is a recognized cause

Correct. Radiation is one of the treatment-related causes of interstitial lung disease of known cause, listed with methotrexate, amiodarone, nitrofurantoin and chemotherapeutics. It is also named among the causes that provoke an inflammatory and fibrotic lung response, so her chest radiation is a credible cause.
No, radiation affects the skin alone

Radiation reaches more than the skin: it is a treatment-related cause of interstitial lung disease and is listed among causes with an inflammatory and fibrotic lung response. Tell: her past chest radiation is a recognized cause of exactly this lung disease.
No, cancer treatment spares the lungs

Cancer treatment does not spare the lungs: both radiation and chemotherapeutics are treatment-related causes of interstitial lung disease. Tell: her treatment history is part of the cause search, and her chest radiation stands out in it.

opts: High-frequency oscillatory ventilation provides no proven benefit even in acute respiratory distress syndrome, where it is listed to avoid. Tell: his severe hypersensitivity pneumonitis calls for corticosteroids, not a ventilator mode.
Return to work with a mask

Continued exposure may lead to a worsened disease state, so going back to the hay keeps the cause in play. Tell: the first step is to identify and avoid the agent, and severe disease then adds corticosteroids.

Correct. After the agent is identified and avoided, corticosteroids may be helpful in severe cases of hypersensitivity pneumonitis, with other immunosuppressants and supportive care such as oxygen. His persistent hypoxia, cyanosis, tachypnea and tachycardia despite avoidance mark severe disease.

Early prone positioning decreases mortality in moderate to severe acute respiratory distress syndrome on mechanical ventilation. Tell: his disease is a hypersensitivity reaction to hay, where severe cases call for corticosteroids.

opts: Acute respiratory distress syndrome develops within 7 days of a known insult, with dyspnea 12-48 hours afterward and new bilateral opacities. Tell: his decline is progressive in a miner, with upper-lung conglomeration rather than new opacities after an insult.

Correct. Progressive massive fibrosis, the complicated form of coal workers' pneumoconiosis, is conglomeration and contraction in the upper lung fields. Complicated cases bring progressive dyspnea, inspiratory crackles, clubbing and cyanosis, the change from his once-simple disease.

Mesothelioma is a primarily pleural cancer nearly always caused by asbestos, and it frequently produces pleural effusions. Tell: his exposure is coal dust, and his film shows upper-lung conglomeration, not pleural disease or an effusion.

About 30% is the overall baseline mortality in this syndrome with low tidal volume ventilation strategies. Tell: his etiology, end-stage liver disease, moves him well above the average to about 80%.
Half is not the figure given for liver failure, which sits at the top of the 20-80% range set by etiology. Tell: end-stage liver disease carries about 80% mortality, the highest named.

Correct. Etiology drives survival in acute respiratory distress syndrome: mortality spans about 20% after trauma to about 80% in end-stage liver disease, against a 30% overall baseline with low tidal volume strategies. His liver disease places him at the high end of that range.

A high antinuclear antibody points to a collagen vascular disease as the cause of interstitial lung disease. Tell: his lung disease is already known to be silicosis, where the arterial blood gas is the contributory laboratory test.

Serum antibodies to an organic agent definitively diagnose hypersensitivity pneumonitis. Tell: quarry dust is inorganic silica, and the useful laboratory study in silicosis is the arterial blood gas, not antibody testing.

opts: One month is too soon: pulmonary function improves over 6 to 12 months after this syndrome. Tell: recovery is measured in most of a year, not weeks, and some functional deficits often remain even then.
Three months falls short of the usual course, which runs 6 to 12 months. Tell: she should expect lung function to keep improving well beyond 3 months, while some deficits may persist.

Correct. Lung function generally recovers over 6 to 12 months after acute respiratory distress syndrome, though functional deficits often remain, with residual diffusion deficits persisting. Physical sequelae after intensive care, such as muscle wasting, weakness and fatigue, also need attention.

Three years overshoots the typical recovery window of 6 to 12 months after acute respiratory distress syndrome. Tell: lasting deficits can remain, but the main recovery of lung function happens within about a year.

How is this pattern classified?
opts: A mixed pattern would need a reduced ratio on top of low volumes. Tell: her ratio of 0.86 sits above the 0.70 normal limit given, so the low capacities stand alone as restriction, the pattern of interstitial lung disease.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. A restrictive pattern is a normal or increased ratio of forced expiratory volume in 1 second to forced vital capacity with decreased total lung capacity and forced vital capacity. Her ratio of 0.86 is preserved while both capacities sit near 60% of predicted, the pattern interstitial lung disease produces.

Her ratio of 0.86 is above the normal limit given, so airflow is not the problem; her lung volumes are what have fallen. Tell: a preserved ratio with a low total lung capacity and forced vital capacity is the restrictive definition.

Her forced vital capacity and total lung capacity are both near 60% of predicted, well under the normal range of 80% or more. Tell: low volumes with a preserved ratio define restriction, which her crackles and dyspnea also suggest.

set2.q: A 46-year-old woman has 1 year of dry cough and exertional dyspnea, bibasilar inspiratory crackles and a restrictive pattern. She has no exposures, medicines, connective tissue disease or sarcoidosis findings, and computed tomography shows fibrosis that does not settle the subtype of idiopathic interstitial pneumonia. Which referral is appropriate?
opts: Lung transplant is listed for severe coal workers' pneumoconiosis and among hypersensitivity pneumonitis treatments, at the far end of care. Tell: she has no diagnosed subtype yet, and the subtype sets her treatment plan and prognosis.
Lung biopsy to define the subtype

Correct. Idiopathic fibrosing interstitial pneumonia may require biopsy for diagnosis, and treatment plan and prognosis depend on the subtype diagnosed. The rule that spares biopsy applies to patients over 65 who meet all four criteria; she is 46 and her scan leaves the subtype open.

Diagnosing idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis without biopsy rests on age over 65 plus all four criteria, including diffuse, patchy fibrosis with pleural-based honeycombing. Tell: she is 46 and her scan does not settle the subtype, so neither condition of that rule is met.

Yearly ophthalmologic evaluation belongs to sarcoidosis follow-up, to identify and manage ocular inflammation. Tell: she has no sarcoidosis findings, and her need is a tissue diagnosis of her idiopathic pneumonia subtype.

set2.q: A 36-year-old woman with interstitial lung disease has a lung biopsy showing T lymphocytes, macrophages and epithelioid cells organized into discrete structures in the lung parenchyma. Which group of interstitial lung disease does this finding place her in?
opts: Correct. Interstitial lung disease falls into two groups: inflammation with fibrosis, and granulomatous reactions. Granulomatous lesions are accumulations of T lymphocytes, macrophages and epithelioid cells organized into discrete structures, granulomas, in the lung parenchyma, exactly her biopsy, as in sarcoidosis.

The inflammation and fibrosis group shows inflammatory cells gathering in the alveolar walls, alveolitis, fibroblasts and collagen deposition. Tell: discrete organized structures of T lymphocytes, macrophages and epithelioid cells are granulomas, the other group.

Pulmonary hemorrhage syndromes, such as Goodpasture syndrome, are alveolar filling disorders with diffuse pulmonary hemorrhage. Tell: her biopsy shows organized clusters of immune cells, not blood filling the air spaces.

Pneumoconiosis is chronic fibrotic disease from inhaled coal dust or inorganic and silicate dusts, as with coal macules. Tell: no dust exposure is described, and her biopsy shows organized granulomas rather than dust-laden fibrosis.

set2.q: A 44-year-old man has had four separate bouts of cough and dyspnea over the past year, each clearing completely between bouts. Which onset pattern of interstitial lung disease does his course fit?
opts: An acute presentation develops over days to weeks and occurs with allergy. Tell: his illness is not one event but four separate bouts over a year that clear completely in between, a recurring rather than a single acute course.

A subacute presentation runs over weeks to months and may occur in any interstitial lung disease. Tell: his symptoms resolve completely between bouts instead of building steadily over weeks to months, which is the episodic pattern.

A chronic presentation runs over months to years and is how most interstitial lung diseases present, including idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and pneumoconiosis. Tell: chronic disease keeps building, while his bouts clear completely in between.

Correct. Interstitial lung disease can present acutely over days to weeks, subacutely over weeks to months, chronically over months to years, or episodically. The episodic pattern of recurrent bouts is less common and can be seen with hypersensitivity pneumonitis, which makes his exposures worth reviewing.

Her arterial oxygen pressure is 51 mm Hg on a fraction of inspired oxygen of 0.90. Which option is reserved for her situation?
opts: Inotrope-driven excessive oxygen delivery causes potential harm, which is why supranormal targets are avoided. Tell: her refractory severe hypoxemia, with a ratio near 57, is a salvage problem, not a target for higher delivery.

A conservative fluid protocol is preferred, because restrictive fluids increase ventilator-free days. Tell: liberal fluids run against that strategy, and refractory severe disease at a ratio near 57 calls for extracorporeal support.

Correct. Her ratio is 51 / 0.90, about 57 mm Hg, well under 100, so she has severe acute respiratory distress syndrome that is refractory to ventilation strategy and prone positioning. Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation is the salvage option reserved for severe, refractory cases.

High-frequency oscillatory ventilation provides no proven benefit in acute respiratory distress syndrome. Tell: switching to an oscillatory mode is listed to avoid, while salvage for refractory severe disease is extracorporeal support.

set2.q: A 67-year-old man aspirated gastric contents during a seizure 2 days ago. His chest film shows new bilateral opacities, and an echocardiogram shows normal cardiac function. His arterial oxygen pressure is 98 mm Hg on a fraction of inspired oxygen of 0.28. How is his oxygenation impairment classified?
opts: Correct. Divide arterial oxygen pressure by fraction of inspired oxygen: 98 / 0.28 = 350 mm Hg. The oxygenation criterion is a ratio under 300, so at 350 he does not meet it yet, even though aspiration of gastric contents is a direct insult and his opacities are new.

Mild covers ratios of 200-300 mm Hg, the least impaired class that still meets the criterion. Tell: his ratio, 98 / 0.28 = 350, is above 300, outside even the mildest class, so the oxygenation criterion is not yet met.
Moderate is 100-200 mm Hg. Tell: 98 / 0.28 = 350, nowhere near 200; the inspired fraction of 0.28 is low, so dividing by it raises the ratio well above the diagnostic threshold.
Severe is a ratio under 100 mm Hg. Tell: an arterial oxygen pressure of 98 is not the ratio; dividing by the fraction of inspired oxygen, 0.28, gives 350, above the 300 threshold.

set2.q: A 72-year-old man with no occupational, drug or connective tissue disease history has 2 years of insidious dry cough and exertional dyspnea. He has bibasilar inspiratory crackles, pulmonary function testing shows a restrictive pattern, chest films over several years show progressive fibrosis, and high-resolution computed tomography shows diffuse, patchy fibrosis with pleural-based honeycombing. How should the diagnosis be established?
opts: Transbronchial lung biopsy or fine-needle node biopsy showing noncaseating granulomas confirms sarcoidosis. Tell: he has no hilar adenopathy or multi-organ findings; his age and honeycombing fit idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, which needs no biopsy here.

Correct. Over age 65, idiopathic disease with inspiratory crackles, restrictive physiology, radiographic progressive fibrosis over several years and diffuse, patchy fibrosis with pleural-based honeycombing on high-resolution computed tomography give idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis with 90% confidence. Such patients do not need surgical lung biopsy.

Idiopathic fibrosing interstitial pneumonia may require biopsy when the picture is incomplete. Tell: he is over 65 and meets all four criteria, which is the situation in which surgical lung biopsy is not needed for the diagnosis.

Antibodies to an inhaled agent in serum give the definitive diagnosis of hypersensitivity pneumonitis, after an organic dust exposure. Tell: he has no exposures, and his findings are the four criteria for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis instead.

set2.q: A 44-year-old woman has interstitial lung disease with a restrictive pattern. She has no occupational exposures, takes no medicines and has no hilar adenopathy. Her clinician wants a laboratory test that screens for a collagen vascular disease as the cause. Which test fits?
opts: An elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme level is seen in 40-80% of patients with sarcoidosis. Tell: she has no hilar adenopathy to suggest sarcoidosis, and the test for collagen vascular disease is the antinuclear antibody.

Correct. A high antinuclear antibody points to the collagen vascular diseases, the connective tissue disorders such as lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren's syndrome and systemic sclerosis that produce an inflammatory, fibrotic interstitial response. With no exposures or drugs, an autoimmune cause is the next to consider.

A positive cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody points to granulomatosis with polyangiitis, a granulomatous vasculitis. Tell: the clinician wants a collagen vascular screen, and the test paired with collagen vascular disease is the antinuclear antibody.

Antiglomerular and antipulmonary alveolar basement membrane antibodies identify Goodpasture syndrome, with glomerulonephritis and diffuse pulmonary hemorrhage in young adults. Tell: she has no hemorrhage or kidney findings, and the collagen vascular screen is the antinuclear antibody.

opts: A conservative fluid protocol is preferred, because restrictive fluids increase ventilator-free days. Tell: fever is treated with antipyretics as part of lowering oxygen demand, not with extra fluid, which runs against the protocol.

High-frequency oscillatory ventilation provides no proven benefit and is listed to avoid. Tell: his agitation and fever call for sedation, analgesia and antipyretics, which reduce oxygen demand directly.

Correct. Reducing oxygen demand in acute respiratory distress syndrome means using sedatives, analgesics and antipyretics appropriately. His fever and agitation both raise oxygen demand, which these measures address while ventilation and positioning support oxygenation.

Inotrope-driven excessive oxygen delivery causes potential harm, which is why supranormal targets are avoided. Tell: the aim here is to lower his oxygen demand, not to push delivery higher with drugs.

set2.q: A 41-year-old cheese maker has recurrent fever, chills, cough and dyspnea hours after handling moldy cheese at work. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is diagnosed, and her symptoms are mild. What is the first step in treatment?
opts: Corticosteroids may be helpful in severe cases of hypersensitivity pneumonitis. Tell: her disease is mild, and without removing the moldy cheese exposure the disease can keep worsening, so avoidance comes first.

Lung transplant sits at the far end of the hypersensitivity pneumonitis treatment list. Tell: her disease is mild and may be reversible if the agent is removed early, so she is nowhere near transplant.

Bronchodilators are supportive treatment, with oxygen and pain medication. Tell: supportive care alone leaves her exposed to the moldy cheese, and continued exposure may lead to a worsened disease state.

Correct. Treatment of hypersensitivity pneumonitis starts by identifying the agent responsible and avoiding it. Prompt diagnosis is key to removing the patient from the irritating environment: symptoms can be reversible if caught early, while continued exposure may worsen the disease.

set2.q: A 61-year-old woman with interstitial lung disease had a chest film 5 years ago showing fine reticular, ground-glass opacities. Her new film shows medium reticular opacities described as honeycombing. How should this change be classified?
opts: Progression from early to late disease

Correct. Among reticular opacities, fine ground-glass change is an early finding and medium reticular change, honeycombing, is a late finding. Moving from ground glass to honeycombing over 5 years marks progression, consistent with fibrosis, which damages the alveoli permanently.
Healing from active to inactive disease

Honeycombing is not a healed state: it is the late reticular finding of interstitial disease, and fibrosis is permanent scar tissue. Tell: her films ran from the early pattern, ground glass, to the late one, which is progression, not recovery.

Coarse reticular opacities are cystic spaces, a separate descriptor from honeycombing. Tell: her film is reported as medium reticular change with honeycombing, the named late finding, not coarse cystic spaces.

Nodular opacities are nodules, and a reticulonodular pattern overlaps reticular shadows with nodules, as in sarcoidosis. Tell: her film shows curvilinear reticular change, honeycombing, with no nodules described.

opts: Genetic predisposition is part of the proposed picture, but it acts together with environmental triggers, and the etiology is listed as unknown. Tell: no single inherited cause is named for sarcoidosis, only a predisposed person meeting a trigger.

Medicines such as methotrexate, amiodarone and nitrofurantoin cause treatment-related interstitial disease, a group of known cause. Tell: sarcoidosis is classed with the interstitial lung diseases of unknown etiology, not with drug causes.

Correct. Sarcoidosis is a multi-organ disease of idiopathic cause, one of the interstitial lung diseases of unknown etiology with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. It is thought to arise from environmental triggers, such as infections, inhaled agents or mold, in a genetically predisposed person, but its etiology remains unknown.

Asbestos fibers cause asbestosis and mesothelioma, interstitial disease of known occupational cause after insulation, demolition, shipyard or construction work. Tell: she has no such exposure, and sarcoidosis sits in the unknown-cause group.

opts: Correct. Her calcium of 11.9 mg/dL is above the 8.5-10.5 range, and hypercalcemia is one of the indications for oral corticosteroids in sarcoidosis. About 90% of cases respond to corticosteroids, so they come first even when the chest film shows hilar adenopathy alone.

Methotrexate, with azathioprine and infliximab, is used when patients are intolerant of corticosteroids or have corticosteroid-refractory disease. Tell: she has not yet had corticosteroids, so an immunosuppressant is the later step, not the first.

Hilar adenopathy alone carries the best prognosis, which can tempt watchful waiting. Tell: her calcium of 11.9 mg/dL is hypercalcemia, a listed indication for oral corticosteroids, so observation leaves an indication untreated.
ruled out by a stated finding

Bronchodilators are a supportive treatment in hypersensitivity pneumonitis, alongside oxygen and pain medication. Tell: her hypercalcemia is a steroid indication in sarcoidosis, and bronchodilators are not among the sarcoidosis treatments.

set2.q: A 46-year-old sandblaster with suspected silicosis undergoes bronchoalveolar lavage. Which lavage finding is expected?
opts: Diffuse pulmonary hemorrhage is the lung half of Goodpasture syndrome, with glomerulonephritis in young adults. Tell: silica produces a thick, milky effluent with foamy macrophages, not blood, and he has no kidney findings described.
Clear fluid with no abnormal cells

A clear, normal return would not match the lavage finding described for silicosis. Tell: silica-laden alveoli give a thick, milky effluent with foamy, lipoproteinaceous macrophages, the result that points to silicosis.
Thick, milky fluid with foamy macrophages

Correct. In silicosis, bronchoalveolar lavage returns a thick and milky effluent containing macrophages that are foamy and lipoproteinaceous. Sandblasting is a free crystalline silica exposure, and the dust deposits in the alveoli, where macrophages invade.

Interstitial infiltrates of lymphocytes and plasma cells with non-caseating granulomas are the histology of hypersensitivity pneumonitis, from organic dust. Tell: his exposure is silica sand, whose lavage is milky with foamy macrophages.

He also has rheumatoid arthritis, and methotrexate he once took for it was stopped after it was implicated in lung injury. His team is weighing methotrexate, azathioprine, infliximab and continued corticosteroids. Which of these should be avoided?
opts: Correct. Methotrexate is one of the immunosuppressants used for corticosteroid-refractory sarcoidosis, but it has also been implicated as a cause of interstitial lung disease, and in him it already was. Azathioprine or infliximab covers the same refractory indication without that history.

Infliximab is one of the immunosuppressants named for corticosteroid-intolerant or refractory sarcoidosis. Tell: nothing in his history counts against it, unlike the drug already implicated in his lung injury, so it remains a reasonable choice.

Azathioprine is named with methotrexate and infliximab for corticosteroid-refractory sarcoidosis. Tell: it carries no prior lung injury in his history, so it stays on the table while the drug implicated in that injury does not.

Cardiac involvement is an indication for oral corticosteroids, and refractory disease is the setting for adding an immunosuppressant to the plan. Tell: nothing in his history rules steroids out; the agent with a record of lung injury in him is methotrexate.

opts: Interstitial markings in the lower lung fields

Correct. In idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis the radiograph shows increased interstitial markings in the lower lung fields, with progressive fibrosis over several areas, matching her bibasilar crackles. Upper lung field nodules belong to coal and silica dust instead.
Nodular opacities in the upper lung fields

Nodular opacities in the upper lung fields, coal macules 2-5 mm across, mark coal workers' pneumoconiosis. Tell: her disease is idiopathic with markings at the bases, not dust nodules at the top of the lungs.
Eggshell calcification of the hilar nodes

Eggshell calcification of the periphery of the hilar lymph nodes is a silicosis finding, from free crystalline silica dust. Tell: that is a lymph node sign of silica exposure, while her disease shows interstitial markings in the lower lung fields.

Bilateral hilar adenopathy alone is stage I sarcoidosis, with no parenchymal involvement at all. Tell: her disease is parenchymal fibrosis with lower-field markings, the reverse of an adenopathy-only film.

About 24 hours later he develops profound dyspnea, tachypnea and crackles, with hypoxemia refractory to supplemental oxygen and new bilateral opacities. An echocardiogram shows normal cardiac function. Which complication of the overdose has he developed?
opts: Correct. Opioid overdose is one of the high-risk drug overdoses that can precipitate acute respiratory distress syndrome, along with aspirin, phenothiazines, tricyclic antidepressants and cocaine. Dyspnea 12-48 hours after the insult, refractory hypoxemia and new bilateral opacities with normal cardiac function fit.

Cardiogenic pulmonary edema shows cardiomegaly, vascular engorgement and batwing perihilar opacities. Tell: his echocardiogram shows normal cardiac function, which excludes the hydrostatic cardiac cause of his opacities.
ruled out by a stated finding

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is a reaction to inhaled organic dust such as moldy hay or bird excreta. Tell: his trigger is an opioid overdose, a listed drug cause of acute respiratory distress syndrome, with no organic dust involved.

Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage is a non-inflammatory intrapulmonary bleeding condition that requires clinical exclusion. Tell: nothing in his case describes bleeding, and his overdose is a recognized trigger of acute respiratory distress syndrome.

set2.q: A 70-year-old man did demolition work around asbestos insulation for 20 years. He now has a pleural effusion, and mesothelioma is suspected. Which test can establish the diagnosis?
opts: Bronchoalveolar lavage returning thick, milky fluid with foamy macrophages is a silicosis finding. Tell: mesothelioma is a cancer of the pleural lining, so the sample comes from his pleural fluid, not from the airways.

A tuberculosis skin test with a current chest film is advised in silicosis because of its tuberculosis risk. Tell: his exposure is asbestos, and his effusion raises a pleural cancer, which is diagnosed from pleural fluid cytology.

A high antinuclear antibody points to a collagen vascular disease as a cause of interstitial lung disease. Tell: an asbestos worker with a pleural effusion and suspected mesothelioma needs the effusion itself examined by cytology.

Correct. Mesothelioma, a primarily pleural cancer nearly always caused by asbestos exposure, frequently produces pleural effusions, and it can be diagnosed from pleural fluid cytology. His long asbestos exposure and new effusion make the fluid the sample to examine.

set2.q: A 63-year-old woman with interstitial lung disease has a computed tomography scan showing established fibrosis with honeycombing. She asks whether the scarring will heal once the inflammation settles. Which response is accurate?
opts: Settling inflammation does not undo scar: the collagen laid down after alveolitis is permanent scar tissue that leaves the lung stiff. Tell: reversibility belongs to early disease caught before scarring, as in hypersensitivity pneumonitis treated promptly, not to established honeycombing.

Corticosteroids appear in the plans for sarcoidosis and severe hypersensitivity pneumonitis, aimed at active inflammation. Tell: the scar itself is permanent tissue, and honeycombing marks late disease, so no medicine is described as dissolving it.

Breathing exercises do not reshape scar: fibrosis permanently damages the alveoli and leaves the lung stiff and restrictive. Tell: rehabilitation appears among supportive measures in pneumoconiosis, which ease symptoms rather than remove scar tissue.

Correct. Fibrosis is the lung's response to an inflammatory source: alveolitis drives fibroblasts to lay down collagen, forming permanent scar tissue that damages the alveoli, stiffens the lung and impairs gas exchange. Honeycombing is a late finding, so her scarring is established and will not heal.

set2.q: A 38-year-old Black woman has a dry cough and dyspnea of insidious onset. She has lupus pernio (painful skin sores on the face), nontender lymphadenopathy and liver and spleen enlargement. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Lupus pernio, painful skin sores on the face, is the skin involvement of sarcoidosis, and a dry cough, insidious dyspnea, nontender lymphadenopathy and liver and spleen enlargement complete its multi-organ picture. Sarcoidosis also occurs more often in Black patients and in women.

Despite the shared word, lupus pernio is a sarcoidosis skin finding; systemic lupus erythematosus is a connective tissue cause of interstitial disease flagged by a high antinuclear antibody. Tell: facial sores with liver, spleen and node enlargement point to granulomas.

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis follows organic dust exposure, with malaise, chills, fever and cough hours afterward. Tell: she has no exposure, and skin sores with liver, spleen and lymph node enlargement are multi-organ findings that dust does not explain.

Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis brings an insidious dry cough with clubbing, inspiratory crackles and pleural-based honeycombing, and its no-biopsy rule applies over 65. Tell: skin sores and liver, spleen and node enlargement point to a multi-organ granulomatous disease.

Pulmonary function testing shows reduced vital capacity and total lung capacity, and his chest film shows pleural plaques with linear streaking at the bases. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Coal workers' pneumoconiosis follows coal dust and shows nodular opacities, coal macules 2-5 mm across, in the upper lung fields. Tell: he never mined coal, and his film shows basal streaking with pleural plaques instead.

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis follows inhaled organic dust, with malaise, chills, fever and cough hours after exposure. Tell: insulation work is an inorganic fiber exposure, and pleural plaques with basal streaking point to asbestos.

Correct. Insulation and shipyard work are asbestos exposures, and patients usually seek attention about 15 years after exposure. Exertional dyspnea with rare cough, fine bibasilar crackles, clubbing, reduced vital capacity and total lung capacity, and pleural plaques, the most common film finding, fit asbestosis.

Silicosis follows silica dust from mining, sandblasting, quarry or stone work and favors the upper lobes, with eggshell calcification of the hilar nodes. Tell: his exposure was insulation in shipyards, and his changes sit at the bases with pleural plaques.

set2.q: A 66-year-old retired coal miner with coal workers' pneumoconiosis and chronic dyspnea asks what can be done for his lungs. He already uses home oxygen and stopped smoking years ago. Which measure belongs in his care?
opts: Early prone positioning decreases mortality in moderate to severe acute respiratory distress syndrome on the ventilator. Tell: he has chronic dust-related fibrosis managed at home, not an acute ventilated syndrome, so positioning has no role here.

Correct. Coal workers' pneumoconiosis has no effective curative treatment, so care is supportive: oxygen, pneumococcal and influenza vaccinations, rehabilitation and smoking cessation, with lung transplant for severe cases. With oxygen in place and smoking stopped, vaccination is the supportive measure still to add.

No effective curative treatment is available for coal workers' pneumoconiosis; care is supportive. Tell: an offer of cure contradicts the disease's management, which centers on oxygen, vaccinations, rehabilitation and smoking cessation.

Avoiding the responsible organic agent treats hypersensitivity pneumonitis, such as farmer's lung or bird fancier's lung. Tell: his disease comes from coal dust, which he no longer inhales since retiring, and moldy hay and birds play no part.
